title: The One Who…
description: One word — اللي — lets you point at anyone or anything by what it does: the guy who works with your uncle, the place we ate at, the thing I told you about. Plus the words for people and things in general, and 'whoever' and 'wherever' for when it doesn't matter which.
approach: Authentic video with scaffolding — a lost-and-found sketch and a 'who's that?' family clip, mined for every اللي, then a describe-and-guess game where you may only use relative clauses.
unlock_condition: Describe three people and two things using اللي correctly with definite heads; ≥8/10 on the اللي / no-اللي quiz
can_do: Describe people and things with 'who / that' clauses
Say 'the one that I…' and 'the thing that…'
Identify people by what they do and where they are from

grammar.title: اللي after 'the', nothing after 'a'
grammar.explanation: Gulf Arabic has one relative word for everyone and everything: اللي. It follows a definite noun — الريال اللي شفته (the man I saw), المطعم اللي رحنا له (the restaurant we went to) — and never changes for gender or number. When the noun is indefinite, there is no اللي at all: ريال يشتغل بالبنك (a man who works at the bank). Inside the clause, the noun is referred to again with a pronoun ending: شفته (I saw him), رحنا له (we went to it) — that little pronoun is not optional. With no noun before it, اللي means 'the one who / whoever': اللي يبي يجي، يجي. Trap: الذي، التي، الذين belong to the news; in the Gulf they are never said.

examples.english: The man I saw yesterday is Kuwaiti

examples.arabic: هذا المطعم اللي قلت لك عنه
examples.transliteration: haadha l-maṭʿam illi gilt lik ʿannah
examples.english: This is the restaurant I told you about
I have a friend who works at the airport

culture.title: Everybody knows everybody — by role and relation
culture.note: In a Gulf city people are placed, not named: the guy who works with your uncle, the one who married the neighbour's daughter, the one from the Eastern Province. Asking منو هذا؟ (who's that?) gets an answer built entirely out of اللي, and you are expected to keep up. The safe way to describe a woman you do not know is by relation — أخت فلان، حرمة فلان — never by looks. When you cannot place someone, the phrase is ما أعرفه، بس شكله من الكويت (I don't know him, but he looks like he's from Kuwait), and no offence is taken.

phrases.arabic: منو هذا؟ — اللي يشتغل مع خالك
phrases.transliteration: minu haadha? — illi yishtaghil maʿ khaalak
phrases.english: Who's that? — The one who works with your uncle
That's the sister of the one who got married yesterday
He looks like he's from the Eastern Province

vocabulary.teaching_note: One form for all genders and numbers, after a definite noun. Written الي online. Trap: الذي / التي are never spoken; never put اللي after an indefinite noun.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman pointing at one man among several at a bus stop; he is holding a red umbrella.

example.english: The phone I bought is expensive

vocabulary.video_hint: Any اللي in description: الشخص اللي، المكان اللي، الشي اللي.

vocabulary.english: the one who / that one which
vocabulary.teaching_note: 'That' plus اللي, for pointing at one of many: ذاك اللي بالثوب الأبيض (the one in the white thobe). Kuwaitis say هذاك اللي, and for a woman ذيك اللي. When you don't point at all, bare اللي does the job: اللي يبي.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand pointing through a crowd at one boy holding a football.

example.arabic: ذاك اللي واقف عند الباب أخوي
example.transliteration: dhaak illi waagif ʿind il-baab akhuuy
example.english: The one standing by the door is my brother

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone picking a person out of a group: ذاك اللي / هذاك اللي.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The all-purpose head when you cannot or will not name the thing: الشي اللي قلت لك عنه (the thing I told you about). Also الشغلة اللي in Saudi and Kuwait. Note شي, never the MSA شيء.
vocabulary.image_scene: A wrapped box on a table with a question mark tag, two people looking at it.

example.english: This is the thing I want

vocabulary.video_hint: Shopping or unboxing: الشي اللي طلبته / اللي أبيه.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The neutral word for a person: شخص واحد (one person), شخص مهم. Plural أشخاص. In casual speech واحد (a guy) and وحدة (a woman) do the same job.
vocabulary.image_scene: A simple outline of a single person standing alone against a white wall.

example.english: The person who called, I didn't recognise

vocabulary.video_hint: شخص in counts (ثلاث أشخاص) and descriptions.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Place in every sense: المكان حلو (the place is nice), مكانك (in your place / instead of you). Plural أماكن. Restaurants and cafés are simply مكان in reviews.
vocabulary.image_scene: A map pin dropped on a coastal café with palm trees.

example.arabic: المكان اللي تغدينا فيه أمس حلو
example.transliteration: il-makaan illi tghaddayna fiih ams ḥilu
example.english: The place we had lunch at yesterday is nice

vocabulary.video_hint: Review vlogs: المكان حلو / المكان اللي.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Gulf spelling and sound — shay, one syllable — never شيء. أي شي (anything), كل شي (everything), ما شي / ولا شي (nothing). Plural أشياء.
vocabulary.image_scene: A tabletop with a phone, keys, a cup and a book scattered on it.

example.english: There's something wrong with the car

vocabulary.video_hint: شي inside فيه شي / أي شي / كل شي.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Mostly in questions and negatives: فيه أحد بالبيت؟ (is anyone home?), ما فيه أحد (nobody's there — also محد). Kuwaitis and Emiratis shorten it to حد. For a positive 'someone' people also say واحد (a guy).
vocabulary.image_scene: A door slightly open with a shadow of a person visible behind it.

example.english: Is there anyone who knows the way?

vocabulary.video_hint: فيه أحد؟ called into a house; محد جا.

vocabulary.teaching_note: أي (any) plus أحد: أي أحد يقدر (anyone can). Also أي واحد. The أي is short and the two words run together: ayy-aḥad.
vocabulary.image_scene: An open call with many hands raised in a crowd.

example.arabic: أي أحد يقدر يجي، الباب مفتوح
example.transliteration: ayy aḥad yigdar yiji, il-baab maftuuḥ
example.english: Anyone can come, the door is open

vocabulary.video_hint: Open invitations: أي أحد / أي واحد يبي.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'The all': الكل جا (everyone came), الكل يعرفه (everyone knows him). Also كلهم (all of them) and كل الناس. Gulf pronounces it kill with a short i.
vocabulary.image_scene: A whole extended family gathered on the steps of a house for a photo.
vocabulary.video_hint: الكل / كلهم in gatherings and gossip.

vocabulary.teaching_note: أي نوع؟ (which kind?), نوع ثاني (another kind), من هالنوع (of this type). Plural أنواع, as in أنواع الناس (types of people), a favourite skit title.
vocabulary.image_scene: Three different dates on a plate — one dark, one golden, one wrinkled — with small labels.

example.english: Which kind of dates do you want?

vocabulary.video_hint: Shopping: أي نوع؟ / أنواع in skits about types of people.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'Every who': كل من يشوفه يقول ما شاء الله (whoever sees him says mashallah). In fast speech bare اللي does the same: اللي يبي يجي. Do not confuse with كل من here as 'from every'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A stream of people at a gate each receiving a date and a coffee cup from a host.

example.english: Whoever came to the wedding ate

vocabulary.video_hint: كل من / اللي as a general subject in proverbs and hospitality.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The question word وين plus ما: وين ما تروح (wherever you go). The same trick makes متى ما (whenever) and كيف ما / شلون ما (however). Said as one word: waynma.
vocabulary.image_scene: A camel silhouette walking across three landscapes — desert, city, sea — in one strip.

example.english: Wherever you go, you'll find Saudis

vocabulary.video_hint: وين ما in travel talk and proverbs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Gulf's warm word for 'a thing': شغلة بسيطة (a small matter), فيه شغلة أبي أقولها لك (there's something I want to tell you). Plural شغلات. Different from شغل (work).
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman leaning in to whisper to a friend, one hand cupped by her mouth.

example.english: There's something I have to tell you

vocabulary.video_hint: شغلة as a vague 'thing' in confidences and lists.

vocabulary.teaching_note: واحد ثاني (another one), مرة ثانية (another time), الشي الثاني (the other thing). Feminine ثانية. The Gulf keeps the th sound — thaani, not taani.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two identical white cups, one hand reaching for the second.

example.english: Give me another one, this one is broken

vocabulary.video_hint: واحد ثاني / مرة ثانية in shops and cafés.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A borrowed word everyone uses: أي ماركة؟ (which brand?), ماركة معروفة. Brand talk is a major Gulf pastime — cars, phones, perfume.
vocabulary.image_scene: A row of perfume bottles with different logos on a glass shelf.

example.english: The car you want, which brand?

vocabulary.video_hint: Car and phone talk: ماركة / ماركات.

vocabulary.teaching_note: أي لون؟ (which colour?), لونه أبيض (it's white). Plural ألوان. Essential for describing a lost item or a car.
vocabulary.image_scene: A paint colour chart fanned out in a hand.

example.english: The bag that got lost is black

vocabulary.video_hint: لون in shopping and lost-item descriptions.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Two syllables in the Gulf: shikil. شكله (he looks like / it seems) is a whole sentence starter: شكله تعبان (he looks tired), شكلها بتمطر (looks like rain).
vocabulary.image_scene: A man squinting at a friend across the room, thinking 'looks tired'.

example.english: He looks like he's from Kuwait, doesn't he?

vocabulary.video_hint: شكله / شكلها as 'it seems' in commentary.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The participle of ضاع: جوالي ضايع (my phone is lost), آنا ضايع (I'm lost / I'm confused). Feminine ضايعة. The lost-and-found desk word.
vocabulary.image_scene: A lost-property counter with a phone, a wallet and keys on a tray.

example.english: The key that was here is lost

vocabulary.video_hint: ضايع in lost-item skits: جوالي ضايع!

sound_spotlight.sound: اللي loses its vowel after a vowel
sound_spotlight.example: هذي اللي، سوي اللي (haadhi lli, sawwi lli)
sound_spotlight.explanation: After a word ending in a vowel, اللي shrinks to lli and glues on: haadhi-lli. After a consonant it keeps its i: ir-rayyaal illi. Listening for the shrunken form is the key to catching relative clauses at speed.

sound_spotlight.example: شفته، رحنا له، قلت لك عنه (shiftah, riḥna lah, gilt lik ʿannah)
sound_spotlight.explanation: The pronoun that points back to the noun is a light -ah or -ha on the end of the verb or preposition. It is always there in Gulf speech, even though English drops it.
'Man' has the ج as y in Kuwait, the UAE, Qatar and Bahrain: rayyaal. Saudis say rajjaal. The clips will have both; it is one word.

lesson_sequence.detail: A 60-second sketch at a mall desk: someone describes a lost bag. Count the اللي you hear.
Eighteen words with audio; the relative phrases show a definite head in colour.
Ten spoken sentence starts (الريال… / ريال…); tap whether اللي follows. Feedback explains definite vs indefinite.
Given a picture and a head noun, build the clause: الولد اللي… with a verb bank; the app checks the resumptive pronoun.
A family photo with five people; hear منو هذا؟ and answer with a role: اللي يشتغل… / اللي تزوج…
Pairs game with the app: describe an object in the room using only اللي clauses until it guesses.
Word counter rolls up. Nudge: describe your phone to yourself with three اللي sentences.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Describe one person in your life without their name: اللي يشتغل… اللي يسكن… اللي دايم…
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen. Three relative clauses with a human head.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Pretend you lost your bag: say its colour, brand and the place you last had it — with اللي twice.
Ask your tutor منو الشخص اللي… about a family member and follow their answer with a second اللي question.
